Holy Boldness
HOH-lee BOHLD-nes
n. phrase
Holy + boldness; renders the Greek parrēsia, “all-saying, freedom of speech, frankness, boldness,” from pas (all) + rhēsis (speech).

📖 Biblical Definition

Holy boldness is the Spirit-wrought, gospel-grounded freedom of speech and conduct by which the believer confesses Christ, prays at the throne, and stands in public witness without the muting fear that natural reluctance, official intimidation, and cultural hostility would otherwise impose. The Greek parrēsia—literally all-saying—is the great New Testament name for the disposition. It belongs first to prayer: seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need (Heb 4:14-16); having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh; And having an high priest over the house of God; Let us draw near (Heb 10:19-22). The atoning work of Christ has secured for the saint a boldness of access to God that no Old Testament saint enjoyed in the same degree. It belongs second to public witness: in Acts the apostles, having tasted the boldness Christ promised His witnesses, speak with parrēsia repeatedly—and when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness (Acts 4:31). It belongs third to the day of judgment: herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world (1 John 4:17)—the saint who is loved and loves can stand before the Judgment Seat without dread. Holy boldness is therefore not a temperamental aggressiveness, not a natural extroversion deployed for kingdom purposes, but a Spirit-given freedom of soul that flows from union with Christ and confidence in His finished work. The temperamentally bold need not assume they possess it (natural boldness in the flesh is not the apostolic parrēsia); the temperamentally retiring need not assume they cannot have it (the Spirit gives boldness to those who pray for it, irrespective of temperament). The church saturated with holy boldness is the church that prays freely, witnesses confidently, and lives without the muting fear of man that would otherwise shrink her.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BOLDNESS as courage; bravery; intrepidity; spirit; fearlessness; in scripture, freedom of speech and confidence of access to God, secured by the atoning work of Christ.

expand to see more

BOLDNESS, n. — 1. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; spirit; fearlessness. 2. Confidence; lack of restraint. 3. Freedom of speech; frankness. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace (Heb 4:16). 4. Forwardness; impudence; want of modesty (the corrupted form).

HOLY, a. — Properly, whole, entire or perfect, in a moral sense. Hence, pure in heart, temper or dispositions; free from sin and sinful affections; conformed in actions to the moral law.

📖 Key Scripture

Hebrews 4:16 — "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."

Hebrews 10:19 — "Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus."

Acts 4:31 — "And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness."

Ephesians 6:19-20 — "And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel, For which I am an ambassador in bonds: that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Holy boldness is corrupted, on one side, by the timidity register that has trained the contemporary believer to mute his confession under cultural pressure—and on the other by the brash-confidence counterfeit that mistakes natural aggressiveness for the Spirit-wrought freedom of speech that flows from union with Christ.

expand to see more

Cultural pressure has produced a generation of believers trained to mute their confession of Christ in public. The fear of social cost, professional consequence, online pile-on, or relational friction has shrunk the apostolic parrēsia to a careful, edited, often apologetic witness that confesses only what is presently culturally acceptable. The recovery is not a temperamental adjustment—making the temperamentally shy into the temperamentally bold—but a Spirit-given gift sought in prayer. The apostles prayed for boldness (Acts 4:29: now, Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word) and were given it; Paul asked the Ephesians to pray that he might speak boldly even from his bonds (Eph 6:19); the church saturated in such prayer is the church given the boldness her testimony requires.

The opposite corruption is the brash-confidence counterfeit, in which natural aggressiveness, online combat-instincts, or temperamental directness are mistaken for the Spirit-wrought parrēsia. The believer becomes loud, contentious, eager for the fight, ready to clip and post and contend, and identifies the resulting cultural-warrior persona with apostolic boldness. The two are not the same. Apostolic boldness is paired with the Spirit’s love and the wisdom from above; it is not the same as raw aggression; it does not despise meekness, gentleness, and the readiness to suffer rather than to inflict; it speaks the truth in love and bears reproach without retaliation. Recover both ends. Refuse the timidity that mutes the confession, and refuse the brash-confidence that mistakes flesh-boldness for the Spirit-wrought freedom. The biblical holy boldness is freedom-of-speech grounded in union with Christ, sought in prayer, deployed in confession and intercession, and married to the Christ-shaped love and meekness that earn the boldness its proper hearing.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parrēsia (literally all-saying; freedom of speech, boldness, frankness)—the Spirit-given freedom of soul by which the believer prays at the throne, confesses Christ publicly, and stands without the muting fear that natural reluctance, official intimidation, and cultural hostility would impose.

expand to see more

Greek parrēsia (G3954) — all-saying, freedom of speech, boldness, frankness (31 occurrences across Acts and the Epistles).

Greek parrēsiazōmai (G3955) — to speak boldly, openly (Acts 9:27-28; 13:46; 14:3; 18:26; 19:8; 26:26).

Greek tolmáō (G5111) — to dare, to be bold (the cousin verb).

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, courageous (the OT cousin of boldness).

Usage

"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace—the atoning work of Christ has secured a boldness of access to God no Old Testament saint enjoyed in the same degree."

"Apostolic boldness is sought in prayer (Acts 4:29) and given by the Spirit (Acts 4:31), not produced by temperamental aggressiveness or natural extroversion."

"Timidity mutes the confession; brash-confidence counterfeits the gift; biblical holy boldness is Spirit-wrought freedom paired with Christ-shaped love and meekness."
